content: Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting infection of the lower respiratory tract. It is more frequently observed in young children and the elderly, particularly during colder seasons. The most common causative agents are viruses, with influenza being a primary contributor. Symptoms typically include cough, sputum production, wheezing, and systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. It is essential to differentiate acute bronchitis from other conditions like pneumonia, asthma, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Management primarily involves reassurance and symptomatic treatment. Preventative measures include proper hand hygiene, vaccination, and environmental control. Smoking cessation significantly reduces the disease's progression and severity. Acute bronchitis was first described by Charles Badham in England in 1808. In 1821, Dr. René Laennec, often referred to as the father of chest medicine, provided a detailed description of the condition. The pathophysiology of acute bronchitis involves the transmission of infectious agents through the large and medium-sized airways, leading to inoculation of the tracheobronchial epithelium. This results in inflammation, thickening of the airway walls, and increased mucus production. Microscopic examination reveals epithelial-cell desquamation, denuding of the airway down to the basement membrane, and lymphocytic cellular infiltration. The most common causes of acute bronchitis include viral infections, bacterial pathogens, and environmental factors. Influenza is a frequent viral cause. In cases of prolonged bronchitis, atypical pathogens such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Bordetella pertussis should be considered. Pneumonia and atypical pneumonia should also be ruled out. The prevalence of acute bronchitis varies depending on the season, vaccination status, and outbreaks during a given year. It is particularly common among young children and the elderly. The primary risk factors for acute bronchitis include age, seasonal variations, and immunization status. If left untreated, acute bronchitis typically resolves within two weeks but may persist for up to two months in some cases. The prognosis is generally excellent, with most patients recovering within 5 to 10 days. However, recurrent episodes of acute bronchitis occur in approximately 20% of patients in subsequent years. The diagnosis of acute bronchitis is primarily clinical, based on history and symptoms. Patients often present with bronchial irritation symptoms such as cough, hoarseness, and sputum production, as well as systemic symptoms like chest pain, fever, malaise, and myalgia. Physical examination findings may include prolonged expiration, wheezing, fever, and abnormal breath sounds. Diagnostic tests are rarely necessary but may include serologic tests, viral cultures, or sputum analysis in specific cases. Inflammatory markers like C-reactive protein (CRP) are often elevated, and procalcitonin can help differentiate bacterial from other causes. Chest X-rays typically show normal lung fields. Treatment focuses on reassurance and symptomatic management. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), albuterol, and antitussives may help alleviate symptoms. Routine antibiotic use is not recommended. However, azithromycin may be used to treat infections caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, or Bordetella pertussis. Primary prevention strategies for acute bronchitis include maintaining proper hand hygiene, controlling environmental exposures, using physical barriers, and vaccinating against preventable pathogens such as influenza and pertussis. Secondary prevention involves smoking cessation or reduction, which can significantly decrease the severity of symptoms associated with acute bronchitis.
